trajectory_summary: The call opens with a soft 'not interested' that quickly reveals itself as genuine cost curiosity, giving the rep multiple live openings to book an appointment. Instead of qualifying or anchoring a time, the rep answers partial financial questions himself with increasingly loose numeric claims, and the call ends with an unanchored 'email me in a week' exit plus a personal-number exchange rather than a locked appointment.
outcome_dispute: The customer never declined the underlying idea of solar — he asked cost questions three times — but the call ends with no appointment, no date/time, and no qualification data collected (no address, no bill, no utility company). This should be read as no_appointment / lead going cold rather than any soft win, because nothing was locked beyond a vague 'I'll email you in a week.'

observed_outcome.reasoning: No day or time was agreed, no verify-section data was collected, and the call ends with the customer's own vague, self-directed follow-up plan rather than any commitment the rep locked in.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The call never reaches a bill-amount or usage question — the conversation stays on cost/price generally and the customer disengages before any verify-section qualification happens.

The customer volunteers general cost curiosity ('Give me a ballpark figure on what it cost') but this emerges organically rather than from the scripted interest question, and the rep never reflects it back as a reason to book.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: unanchored close / no locked next step
primary_coaching_focus.quote: I just I'll email you, in a week.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The call ends with zero verify data collected (no address, no roof, no utility, no bill) and no specific day/time for a callback — just a vague customer-driven 'I'll email you in a week.' This is the single highest-leverage fix: even a rushed customer can be anchored to a concrete callback slot, and without one this lead has no owned next step.

key_moments.quote: Not really interested right now, but
key_moments.stewart_read: This is the textbook 'hello objection' — occurring in the first 30 seconds — and the schema's small-ask template is a direct fit. The rep's actual response at 00:31 ('all we would do is build an estimate... it wouldn't necessarily mean you're committing') is a workable soft-commitment reframe, and the customer does move past the objection on his own by asking a cost question 20 seconds later. But the rep never asks for an explicit small commitment ('30 seconds to explain why I'm calling') — he got lucky that the customer re-engaged unprompted rather than having secured it by design.

key_moments.quote: you're paying nothing out of pocket to get started
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a specific, unqualified financial claim volunteered before any qualification has happened — no address, no bill, no credit check. It edges toward the kind of premature financial commitment the schema's numeric discipline principle warns against, since 'nothing out of pocket' is a claim about the customer's specific situation that hasn't been assessed.

key_moments.quote: I could ballpark it right now, but it could be wrong. And I don't wanna give you a wrong number.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep's underlying instinct (don't give a number) is right, but the phrasing tells the customer a ballpark exists and is just being withheld, which invites more probing rather than closing the door. The canonical redirect frames the appointment as where real, accurate numbers happen — this version frames it as the rep protecting himself from being wrong.

key_moments.quote: Can I reach you back at this number?
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer surfaces a real-world time constraint (an emergency plumbing call) and the rep never anchors a specific callback day/time in response — the call drifts into 'I'll email you in a week' with no rep-owned follow-up plan. This is a soft-exit procedural gap: no locked next step, not a resolved customer objection.
